doc.title: Catherine Russell interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 26, 2018

title: Trying instruments, tuba, and her mother making her find a job
summary: She tried violin, trumpet, saxophone, drums and then tuba; her mother made her find day jobs but cheered the gigs, which paid better.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: That’s right. Was music something that your mother felt okay with you going into?

Yeah. She — well I played violin — you know when music was in schools it was a mandatory thing so you had band, so I played violin. Then I went to — I tried to play everything in the orchestra. So I tried to play the trumpet. Couldn’t do that. Couldn’t get a sound out of the trumpet. I tried saxophone but I didn’t like the vibration on my lower lip and I just couldn’t understand the reeds and that kind of thing. So I went to drums and percussion. First I went to tuba. Because my grandfather played tuba and sousaphone. So tuba was great because the embouchure was loose. I was the bass in the ensemble, like my mom, and I could hide in it. I could wear it. I could get in it. You know it was a big, nice thing. So I really enjoyed that. And I used to, when I started working jobs, because at one point my mother said, “Well you are going to go out of the house and get a job.

Now. Here’s a newspaper and you will find a job.” And I said, “What?” And she said, “No, you’re going to find a job and you’re going to pay half the rent.” So I did that. So I’d come home and say, “Oh, mom, I got a job as a receptionist at Silverstein Properties.” And Silverstein, that was a big company in New York. And she’d say, all right, good. That’s good. And then I’d come home and say, “You know I got a gig. We’re going to play at — ” such-and-such club. She’d go, “Great, great, I’m coming. I’m bringing — ” you know. So it was kind of like that. She was very more excited about the gigs than regular day work.
And often times you might make on a gig what it would take you a day to make —
Oh, a week basically. That was the difference. So music always paid better.
